medical.title: Aficamten trial brings positive news for patients living with non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
medical.summary: Aficamten treatment was associated with significant improvements in symptom burden and exercise capacity in patients with symptomatic non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, according to results presented today in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

medical.title: Mimicry connects smokers and can make quitting difficult
medical.summary: Going out for a smoke together and mimicking behaviors associated with smoking can double tobacco consumption and make quitting more difficult. Researchers from SWPS University examined mimicry as a "social glue" in interactions between smokers and published the results in the International Journal of Psychology.

medical.title: Study tracks early adoption of liver histotripsy treatment
medical.summary: It has been nearly three years since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the HistoSonics Edison histotripsy system to treat primary and metastatic liver tumors. To examine how the technology's adoption and use have progressed, a research team at the University of Virginia, led by Allan Tsung, M.D., professor and chair of the Department of Surgery, sought to provide an early national snapshot of its use for this indication.

medical.title: Healthy lifestyle in early childhood linked to lower risk for IBD
medical.summary: A healthy lifestyle in early childhood is associated with a reduced risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), according to a study published online Aug. 24 in Journal of Crohn's and Colitis.

medical.title: Policy changes could make esketamine more affordable for treatment-resistant depression
medical.summary: A joint research team led by the LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), in collaboration with The Chinese University of Hong Kong, New York University and Newcastle University, has found that a combination of policies and service measures could enhance the value and affordability of esketamine nasal spray, a novel rapid-acting treatment for adults with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in Hong Kong.

medical.title: Focused ultrasound shows safety and feasibility in epilepsy pilot trial
medical.summary: Results from a pilot clinical trial evaluating the safety and feasibility of focused ultrasound neuromodulation in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy were published in Epilepsia. The study, led by Hsiang-Yu Yu, MD, a neurologist at Taipei Veterans General Hospital in Taiwan, built upon the group's initial clinical research with six participants.

medical.title: Not all blood vessel cells respond to injury in the same way
medical.summary: Millions of people worldwide are affected by diseases that cause scarring of the lungs, often leading to breathing difficulties and reduced quality of life. Progressive scarring of the lungs can severely impair breathing and is a hallmark of many chronic lung diseases, most notably pulmonary fibrosis, for which treatment options remain very limited and ineffective.

medical.title: We can eat bread several times a day—as long as it's whole grain, dietitian says
medical.summary: Bread is one of our staple foods, but these days it is also one of the most divisive: some people eat it with everything, while others see it only as a source of carbohydrates and fear it will make them gain weight. According to Adrienn Szabó, it is worth clarifying, first of all, that from an energy perspective, carbohydrates are essential for humans; according to international recommendations, it is best if the largest proportion of our daily energy needs (40% to 60%) comes from carbohydrates.

medical.title: New combination therapy shows promise in metastatic pancreatic cancer
medical.summary: Results from an early-stage clinical trial, published in Nature Communications, showed encouraging outcomes among patients with newly diagnosed cancer whose tumors had spread to distant organs. Most strikingly, one patient experienced a pathologic complete response—meaning no viable cancer cells could be found—and remains cancer-free for more than two years without further treatment. These findings offer an important signal that a new approach may be able to overcome one of the disease's greatest challenges: its resistance to immunotherapy.

medical.title: The hidden role of a cell-cycle regulator in senescent cells that don't divide
medical.summary: In a tale of identities as divergent as "The Prince and the Pauper," a well-known cancer-causing gene also influences cells in a zombie-like state meant to prevent cancer.

medical.title: Short-term pretransplant dialysis does not affect kidney transplant outcomes
medical.summary: Allograft survival is unaffected when kidney transplant (KT) is performed after a short-term pretransplant dialysis duration (PTDD), according to a study published online Aug. 24 in the International Journal of Urology.

medical.title: RSV admissions among infants fall sharply following vaccine rollout
medical.summary: Thousands of infants contract respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) every year. While most experience mild symptoms, the virus can cause severe breathing difficulties in newborns and young infants and may require hospital treatment. Since fall 2025, pregnant women in Denmark have been offered an RSV vaccine to help protect their babies during the first months of life.

medical.title: Reserchers confirm cost-effectiveness of mass hepatitis C virus screening among persons in custody in Hong Kong
medical.summary: A recent study led by the Department of Medicine, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), in collaboration with the Correctional Services Department, has demonstrated that mass screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection among persons in custody (PICs) is a cost-effective strategy. By enabling early identification and treatment of infected PICs, this approach can offer measurable health benefits. The data provide strong evidence to support the implementation of systematic prison-based HCV screening in Hong Kong. The findings are published in The Lancet Regional Health—Western Pacific.

medical.title: Brain recordings hint at how AI reads facial expressions differently from us
medical.summary: The human brain can recognize a person's face and expression in less than a blink of an eye, but current artificial intelligence (AI) models, although fairly accurate at doing the same, use a different process than the brain. That may not be good enough for applications in health care or education, according to new research from York University.

medical.title: The term 'plant-based' diet is ambiguously used in US. Interpretation differs between older and younger adults
medical.summary: When referring to diet, the term "plant-based" has mixed interpretations among U.S. adults, and its meaning varies significantly among demographic groups, according to new research published in the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

medical.title: Three shifting immune states in sepsis could explain why treatments miss their window
medical.summary: Researchers have mapped how the immune response in people with sepsis changes over time. The work, led by King's College London, could help pave the way for treatments that target the specific parts of the immune system that are altered over the time course (trajectory) of sepsis illness in adults.

medical.title: Can total joint replacement particles reach the brain?
medical.summary: Total joint replacement is a proven treatment to relieve chronic knee pain, but concerns have been raised that particles from the device may migrate to the brain and cause memory problems. New research from Rush University shows this may not be a concern.

medical.title: A liver signaling pathway may explain why colorectal cancer weakens muscle and bone
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Indiana University School of Medicine have identified a biological process that may help explain why colorectal cancer can cause severe muscle and bone loss, especially in its most advanced stages. The condition, known as cancer cachexia, can leave patients weak, make everyday activities more difficult and make it harder to tolerate cancer treatment.

medical.title: World's first solar ambulance is energy independent while delivering health care in Kenya
medical.summary: Student team Solar Team Eindhoven from Eindhoven University of Technology has successfully completed the first practical tests of the solar ambulance Stella Juva in Kenya. The ambulance generates more solar energy than it consumes during medical use. This demonstrates that Stella Juva can operate independently without relying on an electricity grid or fuel. To test the delivery of health care powered by the sun, the student team drove to several remote field locations in Kenya.

medical.title: Human blood marker points to a compound that slows ALS in mice
medical.summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a severe neurological disease that destroys nerve cells responsible for muscle movement. The disease typically begins with limb or bulbar weakness and progresses to respiratory failure. Current treatments only modestly slow progression, underscoring the urgent need for more effective therapies.

medical.title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
medical.summary: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long.

medical.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
medical.summary: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.

medical.title: The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels
medical.summary: Samantha Cooper once helped power the oil industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
medical.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

medical.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
medical.summary: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment.

science.title: Rethinking bluegreen aphid control as insecticide resistance spreads
science.summary: When an insecticide application fails to control bluegreen aphid, application conditions may not be the only cause. Research has identified resistant populations across southern Australia, confirming that repeated reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides is no longer sustainable.

science.title: How AI‑powered policing is endangering the public's trust in police
science.summary: Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has dominated the cultural landscape. Uptake across various sectors, including law enforcement, quickly followed, usually with minimal foresight and little to no guardrails, like effective policies or laws, to govern AI use.

science.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
science.summary: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs.

science.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
science.summary: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking.

science.title: Diverse portfolio of protected areas key to Mexican conservation efforts
science.summary: In 2020, Mexico joined 150 nations committing to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 as part of the global 30x30 initiative. More than halfway through the decade, there is ongoing debate about how to effectively expand protected areas to meet that ambitious goal.

Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday to establish the nation’s first U.S. Space Academy. environment.summary: A group of environmental organizations announced their intent to sue the United States National Marine Fisheries Services (NMFS) for failing to consider protections for Eastern Pacific gray whales under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Gray whales (Eschrichtius robustus) are experiencing a potentially catastrophic population decline, a sharp reversal from what had been considered a conservation […]

environment.title: 3,500-year-old skeletons challenge what scientists thought they knew about syphilis
environment.summary: Ancient remains from Vietnam suggest diseases like yaws may have been passed from mother to child thousands of years ago, a form of transmission often assumed to indicate syphilis. The discovery could overturn how scientists interpret ancient infections and complicate the long-running mystery of syphilis’s origins.

environment.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
environment.summary: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

environment.title: “Cannot be explained” – New super steel stuns scientists
environment.summary: Scientists have created an unusually corrosion-resistant stainless steel that could replace costly titanium components used to produce green hydrogen. The breakthrough could reduce structural material costs by roughly 40 times and make seawater-based hydrogen production far more economical.

environment.title: King Harold may have lost England by backing the wrong pope
environment.summary: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

environment.title: 150-million-year-old dinosaur footprints reveal something strange about its walk
environment.summary: A spectacular 150-million-year-old trail of more than 130 footprints captures a giant sauropod making a complete loop before continuing on its way. Its uneven stride hints that the long-necked dinosaur may have been walking with a limp.

environment.title: The secret hidden in these ancient manuscripts isn’t written in ink
environment.summary: Researchers can now recover DNA from centuries-old parchment without damaging the manuscripts, turning historic documents into unexpected genetic time capsules. The hidden clues could reveal ancient trade routes, livestock history, manuscript origins, and details of everyday life stretching back more than a thousand years.

environment.title: Earth’s molten core suddenly reversed direction — and scientists don’t know why
environment.summary: Earth’s molten iron core unexpectedly reversed direction beneath the Pacific, revealing a dramatic change in the hidden engine that creates our planet’s magnetic field. Satellite data suggest the surge is already weakening, raising the possibility that the deep-Earth upheaval is part of a mysterious natural cycle.

environment.title: Scientists find unexpected life on Ötzi the Iceman’s 5,300-year-old body
environment.summary: More than 5,000 years after his death, Ötzi the Iceman is still hosting a remarkable mix of ancient and modern microorganisms. Researchers separated microbes that lived in his body during his lifetime from those that arrived after his death, uncovering traces of his original gut bacteria and cold-loving yeasts that may have survived alongside him in the glacier for millennia.

environment.title: Scientists rediscover lost Megalodon fossils—and reveal a 79-foot giant
environment.summary: Several enormous Megalodon vertebrae thought to have been destroyed in 1989 were found sitting unnoticed on a museum shelf. Their analysis strengthens evidence that the giant shark could exceed 24 meters (79 feet) in length and live for nearly a century. Researchers also estimate that its newborns may have measured an astonishing 3.6 meters (12 feet).

mix_items.summary: Mette-Marit avea 25 de ani, era o mamă singură, necăsătorită, şi o persoană de rând când l-a cunoscut în 1999 pe Haakon, pe atunci prinţ moştenitor al Norvegiei. mix_items.summary: When an insecticide application fails to control bluegreen aphid, application conditions may not be the only cause. Research has identified resistant populations across southern Australia, confirming that repeated reliance on broad-spectrum insecticides is no longer sustainable.

mix_items.summary: Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, artificial intelligence (AI) has dominated the cultural landscape. Uptake across various sectors, including law enforcement, quickly followed, usually with minimal foresight and little to no guardrails, like effective policies or laws, to govern AI use.

mix_items.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
mix_items.summary: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs.

mix_items.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
mix_items.summary: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking.

mix_items.title: Diverse portfolio of protected areas key to Mexican conservation efforts
mix_items.summary: In 2020, Mexico joined 150 nations committing to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 as part of the global 30x30 initiative. More than halfway through the decade, there is ongoing debate about how to effectively expand protected areas to meet that ambitious goal.

mix_items.title: Aficamten trial brings positive news for patients living with non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
mix_items.summary: Aficamten treatment was associated with significant improvements in symptom burden and exercise capacity in patients with symptomatic non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, according to results presented today in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Mimicry connects smokers and can make quitting difficult
mix_items.summary: Going out for a smoke together and mimicking behaviors associated with smoking can double tobacco consumption and make quitting more difficult. Researchers from SWPS University examined mimicry as a "social glue" in interactions between smokers and published the results in the International Journal of Psychology.

mix_items.title: Study tracks early adoption of liver histotripsy treatment
mix_items.summary: It has been nearly three years since the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the HistoSonics Edison histotripsy system to treat primary and metastatic liver tumors. To examine how the technology's adoption and use have progressed, a research team at the University of Virginia, led by Allan Tsung, M.D., professor and chair of the Department of Surgery, sought to provide an early national snapshot of its use for this indication.

mix_items.title: Healthy lifestyle in early childhood linked to lower risk for IBD
mix_items.summary: A healthy lifestyle in early childhood is associated with a reduced risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), according to a study published online Aug. 24 in Journal of Crohn's and Colitis.

mix_items.title: Policy changes could make esketamine more affordable for treatment-resistant depression
mix_items.summary: A joint research team led by the LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), in collaboration with The Chinese University of Hong Kong, New York University and Newcastle University, has found that a combination of policies and service measures could enhance the value and affordability of esketamine nasal spray, a novel rapid-acting treatment for adults with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in Hong Kong.

mix_items.title: Focused ultrasound shows safety and feasibility in epilepsy pilot trial
mix_items.summary: Results from a pilot clinical trial evaluating the safety and feasibility of focused ultrasound neuromodulation in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy were published in Epilepsia. The study, led by Hsiang-Yu Yu, MD, a neurologist at Taipei Veterans General Hospital in Taiwan, built upon the group's initial clinical research with six participants.

mix_items.title: Not all blood vessel cells respond to injury in the same way
mix_items.summary: Millions of people worldwide are affected by diseases that cause scarring of the lungs, often leading to breathing difficulties and reduced quality of life. Progressive scarring of the lungs can severely impair breathing and is a hallmark of many chronic lung diseases, most notably pulmonary fibrosis, for which treatment options remain very limited and ineffective.

mix_items.title: We can eat bread several times a day—as long as it's whole grain, dietitian says
mix_items.summary: Bread is one of our staple foods, but these days it is also one of the most divisive: some people eat it with everything, while others see it only as a source of carbohydrates and fear it will make them gain weight. According to Adrienn Szabó, it is worth clarifying, first of all, that from an energy perspective, carbohydrates are essential for humans; according to international recommendations, it is best if the largest proportion of our daily energy needs (40% to 60%) comes from carbohydrates.

mix_items.title: President Trump Signs Executive Order to Create US Space Academy
mix_items.summary: To strengthen the nation’s space workforce and develop the next generation of space leaders, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday to establish the nation’s first U.S. Space Academy. The order highlights how space is a critical domain for American national security, economic growth, scientific discovery, and technological innovation. The proposed academy […]

mix_items.title: New combination therapy shows promise in metastatic pancreatic cancer
mix_items.summary: Results from an early-stage clinical trial, published in Nature Communications, showed encouraging outcomes among patients with newly diagnosed cancer whose tumors had spread to distant organs. Most strikingly, one patient experienced a pathologic complete response—meaning no viable cancer cells could be found—and remains cancer-free for more than two years without further treatment. These findings offer an important signal that a new approach may be able to overcome one of the disease's greatest challenges: its resistance to immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: The hidden role of a cell-cycle regulator in senescent cells that don't divide
mix_items.summary: In a tale of identities as divergent as "The Prince and the Pauper," a well-known cancer-causing gene also influences cells in a zombie-like state meant to prevent cancer.

mix_items.title: Short-term pretransplant dialysis does not affect kidney transplant outcomes
mix_items.summary: Allograft survival is unaffected when kidney transplant (KT) is performed after a short-term pretransplant dialysis duration (PTDD), according to a study published online Aug. 24 in the International Journal of Urology.

mix_items.title: RSV admissions among infants fall sharply following vaccine rollout
mix_items.summary: Thousands of infants contract respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) every year. While most experience mild symptoms, the virus can cause severe breathing difficulties in newborns and young infants and may require hospital treatment. Since fall 2025, pregnant women in Denmark have been offered an RSV vaccine to help protect their babies during the first months of life.

mix_items.title: Reserchers confirm cost-effectiveness of mass hepatitis C virus screening among persons in custody in Hong Kong
mix_items.summary: A recent study led by the Department of Medicine, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine of the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), in collaboration with the Correctional Services Department, has demonstrated that mass screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection among persons in custody (PICs) is a cost-effective strategy. By enabling early identification and treatment of infected PICs, this approach can offer measurable health benefits. The data provide strong evidence to support the implementation of systematic prison-based HCV screening in Hong Kong. The findings are published in The Lancet Regional Health—Western Pacific.

mix_items.title: Brain recordings hint at how AI reads facial expressions differently from us
mix_items.summary: The human brain can recognize a person's face and expression in less than a blink of an eye, but current artificial intelligence (AI) models, although fairly accurate at doing the same, use a different process than the brain. That may not be good enough for applications in health care or education, according to new research from York University.

mix_items.title: The term 'plant-based' diet is ambiguously used in US. Interpretation differs between older and younger adults
mix_items.summary: When referring to diet, the term "plant-based" has mixed interpretations among U.S. adults, and its meaning varies significantly among demographic groups, according to new research published in the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

mix_items.title: Three shifting immune states in sepsis could explain why treatments miss their window
mix_items.summary: Researchers have mapped how the immune response in people with sepsis changes over time. The work, led by King's College London, could help pave the way for treatments that target the specific parts of the immune system that are altered over the time course (trajectory) of sepsis illness in adults.

mix_items.title: Can total joint replacement particles reach the brain?
mix_items.summary: Total joint replacement is a proven treatment to relieve chronic knee pain, but concerns have been raised that particles from the device may migrate to the brain and cause memory problems. New research from Rush University shows this may not be a concern.

mix_items.title: A liver signaling pathway may explain why colorectal cancer weakens muscle and bone
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz and Indiana University School of Medicine have identified a biological process that may help explain why colorectal cancer can cause severe muscle and bone loss, especially in its most advanced stages. The condition, known as cancer cachexia, can leave patients weak, make everyday activities more difficult and make it harder to tolerate cancer treatment.

mix_items.title: World's first solar ambulance is energy independent while delivering health care in Kenya
mix_items.summary: Student team Solar Team Eindhoven from Eindhoven University of Technology has successfully completed the first practical tests of the solar ambulance Stella Juva in Kenya. The ambulance generates more solar energy than it consumes during medical use. This demonstrates that Stella Juva can operate independently without relying on an electricity grid or fuel. To test the delivery of health care powered by the sun, the student team drove to several remote field locations in Kenya.

mix_items.title: Human blood marker points to a compound that slows ALS in mice
mix_items.summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a severe neurological disease that destroys nerve cells responsible for muscle movement. The disease typically begins with limb or bulbar weakness and progresses to respiratory failure. Current treatments only modestly slow progression, underscoring the urgent need for more effective therapies.

mix_items.title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
mix_items.summary: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long.

mix_items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
mix_items.summary: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.

mix_items.summary: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Sunday, Aug. 30. While you wait to watch the launch, brush up on some key facts about this wide-view mission. mix_items.title: The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels
mix_items.summary: Samantha Cooper once helped power the oil industry. Now she’s fighting to end its hold on our future The post The ex-oil executive trying to wean us off fossil fuels appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
mix_items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

mix_items.title: The dental crown of the future could be 3D-printed while you wait
mix_items.summary: Researchers have found a way to slash the processing time for 3D-printed zirconia crowns from as much as 100 hours to under 30 minutes. The advance could eventually let dentists print strong, customized permanent crowns for patients within a single appointment.

mix_items.title: 3,500-year-old skeletons challenge what scientists thought they knew about syphilis
mix_items.summary: Ancient remains from Vietnam suggest diseases like yaws may have been passed from mother to child thousands of years ago, a form of transmission often assumed to indicate syphilis. The discovery could overturn how scientists interpret ancient infections and complicate the long-running mystery of syphilis’s origins.

mix_items.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
mix_items.summary: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

mix_items.title: “Cannot be explained” – New super steel stuns scientists
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created an unusually corrosion-resistant stainless steel that could replace costly titanium components used to produce green hydrogen. The breakthrough could reduce structural material costs by roughly 40 times and make seawater-based hydrogen production far more economical.

mix_items.title: King Harold may have lost England by backing the wrong pope
mix_items.summary: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

mix_items.title: 150-million-year-old dinosaur footprints reveal something strange about its walk
mix_items.summary: A spectacular 150-million-year-old trail of more than 130 footprints captures a giant sauropod making a complete loop before continuing on its way. Its uneven stride hints that the long-necked dinosaur may have been walking with a limp.

mix_items.title: The secret hidden in these ancient manuscripts isn’t written in ink
mix_items.summary: Researchers can now recover DNA from centuries-old parchment without damaging the manuscripts, turning historic documents into unexpected genetic time capsules. The hidden clues could reveal ancient trade routes, livestock history, manuscript origins, and details of everyday life stretching back more than a thousand years.

mix_items.title: Earth’s molten core suddenly reversed direction — and scientists don’t know why
mix_items.summary: Earth’s molten iron core unexpectedly reversed direction beneath the Pacific, revealing a dramatic change in the hidden engine that creates our planet’s magnetic field. Satellite data suggest the surge is already weakening, raising the possibility that the deep-Earth upheaval is part of a mysterious natural cycle.

mix_items.title: Scientists find unexpected life on Ötzi the Iceman’s 5,300-year-old body
mix_items.summary: More than 5,000 years after his death, Ötzi the Iceman is still hosting a remarkable mix of ancient and modern microorganisms. Researchers separated microbes that lived in his body during his lifetime from those that arrived after his death, uncovering traces of his original gut bacteria and cold-loving yeasts that may have survived alongside him in the glacier for millennia.

mix_items.title: Scientists rediscover lost Megalodon fossils—and reveal a 79-foot giant
mix_items.summary: Several enormous Megalodon vertebrae thought to have been destroyed in 1989 were found sitting unnoticed on a museum shelf. Their analysis strengthens evidence that the giant shark could exceed 24 meters (79 feet) in length and live for nearly a century. Researchers also estimate that its newborns may have measured an astonishing 3.6 meters (12 feet).
